newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KLM profit tumbles as Northwest crutch falls away.
newsitem.headline: KLM profit tumbles as Northwest crutch falls away.

text.p: Dutch carrier KLM Royal Dutch Airlines said Tuesday it fell into the red in the third quarter as operating expenses mushroomed.

A 40 percent higher fuel bill, coupled with increased wage costs, pushed KLM into a third-quarter operating loss of 19 million guilders ($10.3 million). Higher landing fees, air navigation and third party handling charges also contributed to the loss, which compared with an operating profit of 56 million guilders ($30.4 million) a year earlier.

With no further revaluations of KLM's holding in U.S. partner Northwest Airlines to beef up the bottom line, the Dutch flagship carrier also reported a third-quarter net loss of seven million guilders ($3.8 million), down from a 102 million ($55.3 million) profit the previous year.
The results cut the airline's nine-month net profits to 522 million ($283 million), down from 539 million ($292 million) in the year-ago period.
In previous quarters, a steady decline in KLM's operating profits was masked by the revaluation of its equity stake in Northwest. But this process was completed in the first half of 1996-97.
Northwest's contribution this quarter dwindled to just three million guilders ($1.6 million) from 131 million ($71 million) in the previous quarter.
KLM said it was optimistic that its ambitious three-year Focus 2000 restructuring programme would reach its target of boosting annual operating revenues.
"The assessments so far confirm the possibility to structurally improve operating income by 1.5 billion guilders ($813.4 million) over a three-year period," it said.
Projects already being implemented in passenger sales include electronic shopping and the introduction of a new sales and distribution approach.

But industry observers are sceptical, pointing to union reluctance to cooperate on further cutbacks and Tuesday's decision by Dutch travel agents to take KLM to court over its unilateral decision to cut commissions on tickets.
"Pilots, for example, are absolutely not prepared to take a (pay) cut," one analyst said.

KLM said it was maintaining its earlier forecast that full-year 1996-97 net profit before restructuring charges would be about 150 million guilders ($81.3 million) lower than the previous year's record 547 million ($296.6 million).

Contrary to most analysts' expectations, the airline said it would not book its 18.8 percent share of Northwest profits in its final quarter. "The forecast net result for the fourth quarter contains no result from KLM's stake in Northwest Airlines," it said.
